description: Annotated bibliography supporting Vestigium's AI methods. Each entry has a verified DOI or stable URL.
verification: DOIs resolved via Crossref API; arXiv IDs via export.arxiv.org; dataset URLs returned HTTP 200 on 2026-10-22. Summaries come from abstracts or full text where open; licence notes come from host pages and must be rechecked before use.

topics.human_ai_heritage: A. Reference studies: AI for heritage discovery, human–AI evaluation, 3-D
topics.artifact_museum_vision: B. Deep learning on archaeological and museum objects
topics.function_affordance: D. Inferring function from form: use-wear and affordances
topics.shortcuts_leakage_evaluation: F. Shortcuts, confounders, leakage and evaluation
topics.cultural_evolution: G. Phylogenetics, convergence and homology of artefacts
topics.surgical_instruments: H. Surgical instruments: datasets and history

entries.title: Restoring and attributing ancient texts using deep neural networks
entries.authors: Assael Y, Sommerschield T, Shillingford B, Bordbar M, Pavlopoulos J, Chatzipanagiotou M, Androutsopoulos I, Prag J, de Freitas N
entries.implication: Show function hypotheses as ranked candidates with distributions and evidence. Judge the expert+model team against experts alone in a controlled protocol, not by model accuracy alone.
entries.summary: Ithaca is a transformer that restores damaged Greek inscriptions and attributes their place and date. Alone it reached 62% restoration accuracy; historians improved from 25% to 72% when using it. Attribution reached 71% for region, and dates fell within 30 years of ground-truth ranges. It returns ranked hypotheses, distributions over regions and dates, and saliency maps instead of a single answer.

entries.title: Contextualizing ancient texts with generative neural networks
entries.authors: Assael Y, Sommerschield T, Cooley A, Shillingford B, Pavlopoulos J, Suresh P, Herms B, Grayston J, Maynard B, Dietrich N, Wulgaert R, Prag J, Mullen A, Mohamed S
entries.implication: (i) Build retrieval embeddings from heads trained on auxiliary targets (period, source-independent type), not raw generic features. (ii) Evaluate parallels by experts' judgment of 'useful starting point'. (iii) Copy the explicit dedup and modality-leakage reasoning: catalog text that names a function must not be an input when predicting function.
entries.summary: Aeneas restores Latin inscriptions, including gaps of unknown length, and attributes date and place, using the image only for place. It retrieves 'parallels' by cosine similarity on a 'historically enriched' embedding built from the intermediate representations feeding its supervised task heads. In a study with 23 epigraphers, retrieved parallels were useful starting points in 90% of cases. Expert+AI beat either alone on restoration and place. The corpus was deduplicated by identifier plus MinHash/fuzzy matching at >90% similarity, and images were withheld from restoration to prevent leakage.

entries.title: AI-accelerated Nazca survey nearly doubles the number of known figurative geoglyphs and sheds light on their purpose
entries.authors: Sakai M, Sakurai A, Lu S, Olano J, Albrecht CM, Hamann HF, Freitag M
entries.implication: Treat relationship and function suggestions as a low-precision triage queue. Budget review explicitly (suggestions reviewed per accepted finding), report yield by rank, and keep a non-AI discovery channel as a comparator.
entries.summary: A patch classifier was trained on about 400 known relief geoglyphs: 368 train and 33 validation positives, with negatives sampled from their surroundings and heavy augmentation. It was run over 629 km² of aerial imagery. Archaeologists screened 47,410 candidate boxes down to 1,309 high-potential candidates ranked I–III, about 36 suggestions per promising candidate. Field visits to 341 locations confirmed 303 new figurative geoglyphs, of which 178 were individually AI-suggested and 59 were found without AI.

entries.title: Enabling 3D CT-scanning of cultural heritage objects using only in-house 2D X-ray equipment in museums
entries.authors: Bossema FG, Palenstijn WJ, Heginbotham A, Corona M, van Leeuwen T, van Liere R, Dorscheid J, O'Flynn D, Dyer J, Hermens E, Batenburg KJ
entries.implication: Catalog silhouettes are lossy and depend on viewpoint. For a stratified subset of hinged, ratcheted or hollow instruments, 3-D or internal data would test whether 2-D shape similarity holds in 3-D. Estimate scale and pose from in-image references (rulers, markers) instead of assuming them.
entries.summary: Small metal-ball markers scanned with the object let the unknown acquisition geometry be estimated from each radiograph. An algebraic iterative reconstruction (SIRT) then produces CT volumes on uncalibrated 2-D radiography set-ups, shown at the British Museum, the Getty and the Rijksmuseum. The method is not deep learning: geometry is recovered computationally instead of by hardware calibration.

entries.title: The automatic recognition of ceramics from only one photo: The ArchAIDE app
entries.authors: Anichini F, Dershowitz N, Dubbini N, Gattiglia G, Itkin B, Wolf L
entries.implication: Outline-based deep models work for typing when the outline is well defined. Keep silhouette and appearance as separate evidence channels and return top-k candidates for expert confirmation.
entries.summary: Two networks propose pottery types from one field photo: one from the sherd's profile outline (points along inner and outer surfaces), one from decoration. The authors handle scarce labels, extreme class imbalance and rare types. The app proposes candidates and the specialist decides.

entries.title: Applications of deep learning to decorated ceramic typology and classification: A case study using Tusayan White Ware from Northeast Arizona
entries.authors: Pawlowicz LM, Downum CE
entries.implication: Benchmark the model against several independent experts and report expert–expert agreement as the ceiling. Vestigium's pilot review needs at least two independent raters per item.
entries.summary: A CNN assigns sherd photographs to an existing typology with accuracy comparable to, and sometimes above, four expert archaeologists. It also visualises diagnostic design elements and retrieves the most similar sherds from thousands of photos.

entries.title: Deep ancient Roman Republican coin classification via feature fusion and attention
entries.authors: Anwar H, Anwar S, Zambanini S, Porikli F
entries.implication: Fine distinctions such as jaw serration or lock type need local, attention-based features. Test generalisation on held-out types, not only on held-out photos of seen types.
entries.summary: Fine-grained Roman Republican coin types are classified from reverse images using CNN feature fusion and attention. Many classes share the same main motif and differ only in small symbols or legends. A separate disjoint test set, RRCD-Disjoint, contains only classes unseen in training (preprint arXiv:1908.09428).

entries.title: A deep learning approach to fight illicit trafficking of antiquities using artefact instance classification
entries.authors: Winterbottom T, Leone A, Al Moubayed N
entries.implication: CNNs re-identify the same object across photos easily. Views or duplicate catalog records of one object split across train and test will inflate scores. Split by object and duplicate group, and use instance re-identification deliberately as a leakage detector.
entries.summary: Instance classification over 24,502 photos of 4,332 Durham Oriental Museum objects. The exact object was identified about 72% of the time top-1 (up to ~83% with more photos per object, 84% with an ensemble) and about 95% within the top 10.

entries.title: The Rijksmuseum Challenge: Museum-centered visual recognition
entries.authors: Mensink T, van Gemert J
entries.venue: Proc. ACM International Conference on Multimedia Retrieval (ICMR), 451–454
entries.implication: Material, type and date are predictable from museum images, so they can act as proxies for function labels. Rijksmuseum CC0 images are a possible Dutch out-of-collection control set.
entries.summary: A benchmark of 112,039 Rijksmuseum photographs with four tasks: predict artist, object type, material and creation year. Fisher-vector baselines are included.

entries.title: Transfer learning for the visual arts: The multi-modal retrieval of Iconclass codes
entries.authors: Banar N, Daelemans W, Kestemont M
entries.venue: ACM Journal on Computing and Cultural Heritage 16(2):1–16
entries.implication: Cast function labels as retrieval against written, multilingual label definitions (e.g. 'extraction: removal of a tooth, foreign body or fetus'). This makes label semantics explicit and auditable and allows zero- or few-shot labels.
entries.summary: A fully fine-tunable retrieval framework assigns Iconclass codes to artworks. Multilingual titles and image features are matched against the textual definitions of the codes, which addresses many labels with little training data.

entries.title: A multimodal turn in Digital Humanities. Using contrastive machine learning models to explore, enrich, and analyze digital visual historical collections
entries.authors: Smits T, Wevers M
entries.implication: CLIP zero-shot queries suit exploration but carry modern-web priors, such as mapping antique objects onto modern categories. Audit them before using any output as evidence.
entries.summary: Three case studies show CLIP-style models supporting text-to-image, image-to-image and zero-shot exploration of historical visual collections. The authors warn of historical bias inherited from web training data.

entries.title: Beyond Accuracy: Investigating Vision Model Perception on 19th-Century Decorative Arts
entries.authors: Toumarkine A, Vidal-Gorène C
entries.venue: Anthology of Computers and the Humanities 3
entries.implication: Direct evidence that off-the-shelf embeddings of heritage photos encode photographic framing. Test image retrieval on masked and background-normalised crops and publish attribution maps.
entries.summary: VGG16, EfficientNet, ViT, DINOv2 and CLIP are compared for zero-shot clustering and similarity retrieval on 19th-century decorative arts, with aggregated activation maps. The models often attended to background contrast and image framing rather than decorative structure.

entries.title: Momocs: Outline analysis using R
entries.authors: Bonhomme V, Picq S, Gaucherel C, Claude J
entries.implication: A reference implementation for cross-checking Vestigium's Fourier shape block, and the interpretable baseline any learned silhouette embedding must beat.
entries.summary: An R package for outline morphometrics: elliptic Fourier and related descriptors, normalisation for size, rotation and starting point, and PCA/LDA in a reproducible pipeline.

entries.title: Archaeology, biology, and borrowing: A critical examination of Geometric Morphometrics in Archaeology
entries.authors: Okumura M, Araujo AGM
entries.implication: Corresponding points on tools (jaw tip, pivot, handle end) are design or functional correspondences, not biological homologies. Define them explicitly and keep homology language out of shape outputs.
entries.summary: A critique of how archaeology has borrowed geometric morphometrics. Biological concepts such as landmark homology, modularity and allometry are often applied to artefacts without justification.

entries.title: LUWA Dataset: Learning Lithic Use-Wear Analysis on Microscopic Images
entries.authors: Zhang J, Fang I, Wu H, Kaushik A, Rodriguez A, Zhao H, Zhang J, Zheng Z, Iovita R, Feng C
entries.implication: Function is best evidenced by use-traces under controlled experiments, which catalog thumbnails cannot show. Function inferred from form must stay a hypothesis, and imaging modality and scale must be stratified as confounders.
entries.summary: An open dataset of 23,130 microscopic images of experimentally used stone tools, labelled by worked material, across magnifications and sensing modalities. Pretrained models including DINOv2 and few-shot methods are benchmarked. They beat human experts but leave a large gap, and imaging conditions are strong confounders.

entries.title: Classifying polish in use-wear analysis with convolutional neural networks
entries.authors: Eleftheriadou A, Djellal Y, McPherron SP, Marreiros J
entries.implication: Pretrained features are not automatically better for small, domain-specific data. Keep a small-capacity or from-scratch baseline and test crop size and resolution.
entries.summary: CNNs classify experimental use-wear polish by contact material (wood, hide, bone) and by duration of use. Bone and hide were classified well and wood poorly. Custom models beat pretrained ones on small surface patches, and image scale mattered.

entries.title: Affordance detection of tool parts from geometric features
entries.authors: Myers A, Teo CL, Fermüller C, Aloimonos Y
entries.implication: Function belongs to parts (blade, jaws, handle), and a part can carry several ranked affordances. This supports multi-label, part-localised hypotheses rather than single whole-object labels.
entries.summary: Introduces the UMD RGB-D part-affordance dataset: 105 kitchen, workshop and garden tools with pixel labels for grasp, cut, scoop, contain, pound, support and wrap-grasp, plus ranked affordances per part. Part affordances are detected from local geometric features.

entries.title: Understanding tools: Task-oriented object modeling, learning and recognition
entries.authors: Zhu Y, Zhao Y, Zhu S-C
entries.implication: Functional equivalence comes from mechanism (contact geometry, force, action), not visual likeness. Tie Vestigium's function labels to explicit mechanical criteria such as pivot or lever, jaw opposition and edge, so they can be checked.
entries.summary: Tools are modelled by four components: a grasp region, a functional region acting on the target, an imagined action trajectory, and the physical quantity produced (force, pressure). Learning from one RGB-D demonstration, the model picks substitute tools, including stones, for new tasks.

entries.title: A model-based approach to finding substitute tools in 3D vision data
entries.authors: Abelha P, Guerin F, Schoeler M
entries.implication: Gives an operational, part-parametric definition of functional similarity, distinct from overall visual similarity. A working-end descriptor comparison is a principled baseline for function-oriented retrieval.
entries.summary: Candidate objects are segmented into parts and each part is fitted with a superquadric. Part parameters are compared with those the task requires, to find tools that can substitute for a missing one.

entries.title: Learning transferable visual models from natural language supervision
entries.authors: Radford A, Kim JW, Hallacy C, Ramesh A, Goh G, Agarwal S, Sastry G, Askell A, Mishkin P, Clark J, Krueger G, Sutskever I
entries.implication: A baseline for zero-shot function prompts and image–text retrieval. The training data are undisclosed, so prior exposure to museum images cannot be ruled out, and zero-shot results are not independent evidence.
entries.summary: Contrastive image–text pretraining on 400M web pairs, enabling zero-shot transfer through text prompts.

entries.title: Reproducible scaling laws for contrastive language-image learning
entries.authors: Cherti M, Beaumont R, Wightman R, Wortsman M, Ilharco G, Gordon C, Schuhmann C, Schmidt L, Jitsev J
entries.implication: Known pretraining data make it possible to check for contamination, e.g. whether collection images appear in LAION. Prefer it over closed CLIP for reproducibility.
entries.summary: An open reproduction of CLIP training on public LAION data, with scaling laws, open code and open weights (OpenCLIP).

entries.title: Sigmoid loss for language image pre-training
entries.authors: Zhai X, Mustafa B, Kolesnikov A, Beyer L
entries.implication: Suited to contrastive fine-tuning on only ~2.8k image–text pairs. SigLIP 2's multilingual text tower is relevant to Dutch and Swedish catalog text.
entries.summary: Replaces the batch-softmax contrastive loss with an independent pairwise sigmoid loss, which works well at small batch sizes. SigLIP 2 (Tschannen et al. 2025, arXiv:2502.14786) adds multilingual training and better dense features.

entries.title: DINOv2: Learning robust visual features without supervision
entries.authors: Oquab M, Darcet T, Moutakanni T, Vo H, Szafraniec M, Khalidov V, Fernandez P, Haziza D, Massa F, El-Nouby A, et al.
entries.implication: The default frozen image backbone to replace the ImageNet ResNet18 baseline. Evaluate it frozen (kNN, linear probe) before any fine-tuning.
entries.summary: Self-supervised ViTs trained on 142M curated images give strong frozen features for classification, retrieval and dense tasks; code and weights are Apache-2.0. DINOv3 (Siméoni et al. 2025, arXiv:2508.10104) scales this up under a custom, gated licence.

entries.title: BioCLIP: A vision foundation model for the tree of life
entries.authors: Stevens S, Wu J, Thompson MJ, Campolongo EG, Song CH, Carlyn DE, Dong L, Dahdul WM, Stewart C, Berger-Wolf T, Chao W-L, Su Y
entries.implication: A template for putting a label hierarchy (family → type → variant, or function → mechanism) into text supervision. The resulting hierarchy reflects the labels supplied, not a discovered genealogy.
entries.summary: A CLIP model trained on TreeOfLife-10M with taxonomic name strings as text. It gains 16–17 points absolute on fine-grained biology tasks, and its embedding forms a hierarchy that matches the taxonomy.

entries.title: On the effectiveness of ViT features as local semantic descriptors (arXiv: Deep ViT features as dense visual descriptors)
entries.authors: Amir S, Gandelsman Y, Bagon S, Dekel T
entries.implication: Enables part-aware comparison (jaws to jaws, handles to handles) without part labels. Compute working-end similarity separately from handles and decoration.
entries.summary: Patch features from self-supervised DINO-ViT encode localised, part-level semantics that are shared across related categories. Simple clustering of these features gives zero-shot co-segmentation, part co-segmentation and semantic correspondence (arXiv:2112.05814).

entries.title: Robust fine-tuning of zero-shot models
entries.authors: Wortsman M, Ilharco G, Kim JW, Li M, Kornblith S, Roelofs R, Gontijo Lopes R, Hajishirzi H, Farhadi A, Namkoong H, Schmidt L
entries.implication: When fine-tuning on few Vestigium pairs, interpolate with zero-shot weights. Report performance on held-out sources (a real distribution shift), not only random splits.
entries.summary: WiSE-FT averages the weights of a zero-shot model and its fine-tuned version. This keeps robustness to distribution shift while gaining in-distribution accuracy.

entries.title: Making monolingual sentence embeddings multilingual using knowledge distillation
entries.authors: Reimers N, Gurevych I
entries.implication: Add a multilingual encoder alongside TF-IDF so Dutch, Swedish and English descriptions of similar objects align. Test explicitly whether text clusters are really language or museum clusters.
entries.summary: Multilingual sentence encoders are distilled from a monolingual teacher using translated pairs, aligning 50+ languages in one space.

entries.title: Shortcut learning in deep neural networks
entries.authors: Geirhos R, Jacobsen J-H, Michaelis C, Zemel R, Brendel W, Bethge M, Wichmann FA
entries.implication: Make out-of-distribution tests (leave-one-museum-out, leave-one-photo-campaign-out) primary evidence, not appendices.
entries.summary: Defines shortcut learning: decision rules that score well on standard benchmarks but fail under distribution shift. The authors recommend out-of-distribution tests as standard practice.

entries.title: Unmasking Clever Hans predictors and assessing what machines really learn
entries.authors: Lapuschkin S, Wäldchen S, Binder A, Montavon G, Samek W, Müller K-R
entries.implication: Museum thumbnails contain rulers, accession labels, colour charts, mounts and watermarks. Cluster relevance maps to find neighbours or labels driven by these artefacts.
entries.summary: Relevance maps (LRP) and Spectral Relevance Analysis (SpRAy) expose 'Clever Hans' strategies, such as a PASCAL VOC horse classifier keying on a source watermark. Standard accuracy metrics cannot tell these strategies apart.

entries.title: Variable generalization performance of a deep learning model to detect pneumonia in chest radiographs: A cross-sectional study
entries.authors: Zech JR, Badgeley MA, Liu M, Costa AB, Titano JJ, Oermann EK
entries.implication: A direct analogue of the museum confound. If function base rates differ by source, source-identifying features will 'predict' function. Measure how well each embedding predicts source, and report function results within and across sources.
entries.summary: CNNs trained on 158,323 radiographs from three hospital systems generalised worse to external sites. They could identify the source hospital and department very accurately and exploited prevalence differences between sites.

entries.title: Unbiased look at dataset bias
entries.authors: Torralba A, Efros AA
entries.implication: Run 'Name That Museum': a linear probe predicting source collection from each representation. High accuracy flags bias that retrieval must control, e.g. by source-stratified or cross-source neighbours.
entries.summary: In the 'Name That Dataset' test, classifiers easily identify which benchmark an image came from, and cross-dataset generalisation drops substantially.

entries.title: Noise or signal: The role of image backgrounds in object recognition
entries.authors: Xiao K, Engstrom L, Ilyas A, Madry A
entries.implication: Build background-only, foreground-only (masked) and swapped-background variants of collection images to measure how much retrieval depends on background.
entries.summary: A toolkit separating foreground from background on ImageNet. Models reach non-trivial accuracy from backgrounds alone, and adversarial backgrounds flip up to 87.5% of correctly classified foregrounds. More accurate models rely less on backgrounds.

entries.title: ImageNet-trained CNNs are biased towards texture; increasing shape bias improves accuracy and robustness
entries.authors: Geirhos R, Rubisch P, Michaelis C, Bethge M, Wichmann FA, Brendel W
entries.implication: The field disagrees, so do not assume which cues a model uses on metal instruments (patina, finish, colour or outline). Measure it on Vestigium data with silhouette-only, grayscale and texture-scrambled inputs.
entries.summary: Cue-conflict experiments indicate that ImageNet CNNs favour texture over shape, and training on Stylized-ImageNet raises shape bias. Counterpoint: Burgert, Stoll, Rota & Demir (NeurIPS 2025, https://doi.org/10.52202/085713-2033) use controlled cue suppression and find reliance mainly on local shape, varying by domain.

entries.title: Leakage and the reproducibility crisis in machine-learning-based science
entries.authors: Kapoor S, Narayanan A
entries.implication: Complete a model info sheet per experiment. Labels derived from catalog text, evaluated by a model that also sees that text, are a textbook leakage case.
entries.summary: Finds leakage in 294 papers across 17 fields, gives a taxonomy of eight leakage types, and proposes 'model info sheets'. In a corrected civil-war-prediction case, complex models were no better than logistic regression.

entries.title: Do we train on test data? Purging CIFAR of near-duplicates
entries.authors: Barz B, Denzler J
entries.implication: Run perceptual-hash and embedding near-duplicate detection across all sources (re-used thumbnails, the same object in several catalogs). Report scores with and without near-duplicate pairs.
entries.summary: Near-duplicates of training images make up 3.3% (CIFAR-10) and 10% (CIFAR-100) of test images. Replacing them lowered accuracy by 9–14% relative.

entries.title: A metric learning reality check
entries.authors: Musgrave K, Belongie S, Lim S-N
entries.implication: Fix hyperparameters on validation data only, match embedding size and augmentation, and report rank-aware metrics (MAP@R, recall@k) against simple baselines (TF-IDF, Fourier).
entries.summary: Finds methodological flaws in metric-learning papers, including unequal settings and tuning on test data. Under fair comparison, gains were marginal. Proposes MAP@R.

entries.title: Similarity of neural network representations revisited
entries.authors: Kornblith S, Norouzi M, Lee H, Hinton G
entries.implication: Without ground truth, compare text, shape and image representations with CKA and k-NN overlap, and against nuisance representations (source ID, photo statistics), to see what each embedding mainly encodes.
entries.summary: Introduces centered kernel alignment (CKA), a reliable measure of similarity between representations that is invariant to orthogonal transforms and isotropic scaling.

entries.title: Multi-label learning from single positive labels
entries.authors: Cole E, Mac Aodha O, Lorieul T, Perona P, Morris D, Jojic N
entries.implication: The formal counterpart of Vestigium's 'missing = unknown' rule. Never train with assumed negatives; use partial-label losses and report how many positives each label had.
entries.summary: Studies multi-label training where each image has one confirmed positive and all other labels are unobserved. Treating unobserved labels as negatives hurts; expected-positive regularisation and label estimation help.

entries.title: Conformal prediction: A gentle introduction
entries.authors: Angelopoulos AN, Bates S
entries.venue: Foundations and Trends in Machine Learning 16(4):494–591
entries.implication: Once an adjudicated calibration set exists, turn neighbour-vote scores into label sets with stated coverage and explicit abstention; until then they remain uncalibrated. Exchangeability likely fails across museums, so check coverage per source.
entries.summary: A tutorial on conformal prediction: prediction sets with distribution-free, finite-sample coverage under exchangeability, given a held-out calibration set. Extensions cover multi-label prediction and risk control.

entries.title: Cladistics is useful for reconstructing archaeological phylogenies: Palaeoindian points from the southeastern United States
entries.authors: O'Brien MJ, Darwent J, Lyman RL
entries.implication: Any lineage claim needs explicitly coded characters, a rationale for polarity or outgroup, and homoplasy statistics. Trees built from embedding distances are not phylogenies.
entries.summary: Applies parsimony cladistics to Paleoindian projectile points coded as discrete character states. Homoplasy is quantified, and the resulting trees are treated as testable hypotheses of descent.

entries.title: Phylogenetics and material cultural evolution
entries.authors: Tëmkin I, Eldredge N
entries.implication: Instrument designs spread through makers, trade catalogs and copying (reticulation). Represent relationships as networks anchored in documented maker and designer links, such as the Boerhaave designer–maker tables, not as similarity trees.
entries.summary: Compares the evolution of designed artefacts (musical-instrument case studies) with biological phylogenetics. Horizontal transfer, blending and deliberate design break the assumptions of branching-tree models, so tree reconstructions of material culture need caution and alternative representations.

entries.title: Convergent Evolution in Stone-Tool Technology
entries.authors: O'Brien MJ, Buchanan B, Eren MI (eds.)
entries.venue: MIT Press (Vienna Series in Theoretical Biology)
entries.implication: Strong functional constraints (e.g. gripping needs opposed jaws and a pivot) predict convergent form. Roman–modern similarity is expected from function alone and is not evidence of descent unless independent historical evidence supports it.
entries.summary: An edited volume showing that similar stone-tool forms often arise independently under shared functional and material (fracture-mechanics) constraints. Replication experiments and phylogenetic methods are used to judge how likely convergence is.

entries.title: Surgical tool datasets for machine learning research: A survey
entries.authors: Rodrigues M, Mayo M, Patros P
entries.implication: Few public datasets show isolated instruments in catalog-like views. Modern links rest on small tray or catalog sets, so their sizes and photographic domains must be reported.
entries.summary: A survey of surgical-tool datasets, tasks (detection, segmentation, tracking), metrics and deep-learning methods, with a taxonomy of approaches. The data are dominated by endoscopic and laparoscopic video.

entries.title: Labeled Surgical Tools and Images [dataset]
entries.authors: Lavado D, da Silva J, Caramelo F
entries.venue: Kaggle (University of Coimbra MSc project); ODbL v1.0 per Dataset Ninja mirror
entries.implication: A small modern reference set for checking whether embeddings place modern scissors and clamps near historical cutting and gripping instruments. The tray background is itself a domain confound.
entries.summary: About 2,620 images with 3,639 boxes (one listing says 3,009 images) of four classes: scalpel no. 4, straight dissection clamp, and straight and curved Mayo scissors. Tools lie on a cluttered tray under varied rotation, tilt and lighting, with occlusion flags.

entries.title: Real-time ultra-fine-grained surgical instrument classification
entries.authors: Atabuzzaman M, DiMatteo G, Alomari H, Tang C, Hale C, Goode AE, King DR, Thomas C
entries.implication: Near-identical modern variants need multiple controlled views. With single catalog thumbnails, report modern–historical matches at family level, not exact model.
entries.summary: Multi-view CNN and transformer models classify 95 instrument classes from three standard trays in a hospital sterile-services setting, followed by a post-deployment user study.

entries.title: EndoNet: A deep architecture for recognition tasks on laparoscopic videos
entries.authors: Twinanda AP, Shehata S, Mutter D, Marescaux J, de Mathelin M, Padoy N
entries.implication: Contrast only. Instruments in use (tips, blur, tissue) look nothing like catalog photographs, so these data are unsuitable for function transfer. They do show what direct in-use evidence looks like.
entries.summary: A multi-task CNN for surgical phase recognition and tool presence in laparoscopic video, introducing Cholec80 (80 cholecystectomies; tool presence at 1 fps; CC BY-NC-SA 4.0). Related segmentation benchmark: EndoVis 2017 (Allan et al., arXiv:1902.06426).

entries.title: The Tools of Asclepius: Surgical Instruments in Greek and Roman Times
entries.authors: Bliquez LJ
entries.implication: An independent, non-image evidence channel for Roman instrument function, and a basis for adjudication rubrics. Its typology is expert input and must not be presented as a model discovery.
entries.summary: The standard modern reference on Greco-Roman surgical instruments, organised by period and instrument category and combining ancient texts with archaeological finds.
